content:
Apple is facing a surge in "AI slop" security reports and has recently made adjustments to its bug bounty program. Here are the details.

Apple limits unprocessed vulnerability report numbers

Apple confirmed to the Financial Times that it has "introduced submission caps and a thirty-day cooling-off period on its internal security portal, requiring users to apply for an increase in quota."

The measures were implemented in June and aim to address the surge in vulnerability reports across the industry—as large language models become increasingly capable, they can find, string together, and exploit vulnerabilities, making it difficult for review teams to keep up with the volume of submissions.

A few weeks ago, Apple confirmed that in response to these AI tools, it was accelerating the rollout of security updates, releasing patches originally planned for last week's 26.6 update earlier in iOS 26.5.2 and its corresponding versions.

In the security notes for all of these systems, Apple acknowledged researchers who used AI tools from companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Z.ai, thanking them for their help in discovering multiple vulnerabilities.

One of the teams acknowledged was Calif.io, which said in May that using Anthropic's Mythos Preview model, they had built a working macOS kernel memory corruption exploit on the M5 chip in just five days.

The Financial Times report came out a few days ago, and GitHub also earlier rolled out a tiered system for its bug bounty program to curb AI slop reports while distinguishing submissions from certified security researchers.

The Financial Times report tells the story of Bynario, a seven-person cybersecurity startup. The company has used AI tools and models in recent years to find vulnerabilities; this year it submitted five vulnerabilities to Apple that were blocked, while last year it submitted eight, "one of which was patched in a November software update."

After the Financial Times report, Apple has since reached out to Bynario and reviewed its findings, which included a potential privilege escalation exploit chain that could give attackers full control of a Mac.

Apple issued a statement to the Financial Times regarding the recent bug bounty program adjustments:

The company added that researchers "can easily apply to raise their limit at any time, ensuring important reports reach our security team."
